rationale: The recordings have no artifact rejection, and the external clinic uses a different reference. I'm making one robustness change to how spectra are estimated: re-reference each recording to the common average, then take the median across Welch segments instead of the mean. Blinks, movement and electrode pops then can't dominate the per-channel spectra, and the spatial pattern no longer depends on the original reference. Features and classifier stay the same, so any change in score comes from cleaner spectra.

Split the broad alpha and beta bands into physiologically distinct sub-bands: low alpha 8–10 Hz and high alpha 10–13 Hz, plus beta1 13–20 Hz and beta2 20–30 Hz. MDD and its medication effects are reported to sit in specific sub-bands, such as high-alpha changes and excess fast beta from benzodiazepines and antidepressants, and these get averaged away in the 5-band summary. Everything else is unchanged: the original reference, mean Welch, log relative power and the same logistic regression. Round 1 showed that changing the reference and spectral estimator hurt a lot.

The current model only uses per-channel relative power, so it can't see the spatial covariance structure: interhemispheric and frontal coupling, which MDD is reported to alter. I'm adding a 1–45 Hz covariance matrix per condition, shrunk with OAS (Oracle Approximating Shrinkage) and divided by its trace so overall amplitude doesn't matter. Each matrix is projected to the Riemannian tangent space at the training-fold mean. These features go alongside the existing log relative band powers, with the same standardized L2 logistic regression.

Adding the broadband covariance gave the biggest gain so far, but a single 1–45 Hz matrix is dominated by high-power alpha. That hides changes in coupling that are specific to one frequency band, such as frontal/interhemispheric theta, alpha and beta connectivity, which are reported in MDD. I'm adding OAS-shrunk, trace-normalized covariances for theta (4–8 Hz), alpha (8–13 Hz) and beta (13–30 Hz) alongside the broadband one. Each condition and band gets its own Riemannian tangent space at the training-fold mean; the band powers and the standardized L2 logistic regression stay the same.

Rounds 3–4 added 8 tangent-space blocks, so the model now has about 1,710 standardized features (8 × 190 covariance terms plus 190 band powers) for only a few hundred subjects. A fixed C=0.1 was chosen when there were only 190 features and is probably too weak for this many. I'm selecting C (searched from 1e-4 to 1) by AUROC with 5-fold grouped inner CV on each training fold, grouped by `groups_train`, so the amount of shrinkage matches the dimensionality. Features and model family are otherwise unchanged.

I'm completing the filter-bank covariance set by adding delta (1–4 Hz) and low-gamma (30–45 Hz) covariances per condition, each in its own Riemannian tangent space. Hegerl's vigilance model links MDD to differences in slow-wave coupling, and fast beta/gamma coupling reflects antidepressant and benzodiazepine effects and muscle tension. The two bands where the current model has no coupling information are the ones where these effects should show up.

The single L2 logistic regression is fitted on about 1,710 standardized features (band powers plus 8 tangent-space blocks) from only a few hundred subjects. That makes it high-variance, and adding more blocks has started to hurt (round 6). I'm replacing it with a fixed, untuned ensemble: one logistic regression per feature block (band power, and each condition × band covariance), all at C=0.1, the setting chosen when the model had 190 features. Their log-odds are averaged. Each band and condition's coupling pattern then votes separately, which should cut variance without adding features or tuning anything against the score.

I'm adding one new feature family, the aperiodic (1/f) exponent, alongside the current band powers and covariances. For each channel and condition, I fit a line to log power vs. log frequency over 2–7 Hz and 14–40 Hz, skipping the alpha peak and line noise. The 1/f slope is a proposed marker of excitation/inhibition balance and is reported to change in MDD. Relative power and trace-normalized covariances can't see it, and because the slope ignores amplitude scale it should carry over to other amplifiers. This adds only 38 features, so there is little extra overfitting risk.

I'm adding Higuchi fractal dimension per channel and condition, computed on the 1–45 Hz signal, as a new non-linear complexity feature. Several studies report that it separates MDD from controls, and it measures waveform irregularity that band powers, the 1/f slope and covariances can't capture. It doesn't depend on amplitude scale, so it should carry over to other amplifiers, and it adds only 38 features.

I'm adding one value per channel and condition: the individual alpha frequency, taken as the power-weighted centre of gravity of the 7–13 Hz Welch PSD. The model can't build this from its current features, which are fixed-band relative powers, a 1/f slope, fractal dimension and covariances; it can only be estimated from the shape of the spectrum. Alpha slowing and differences in alpha frequency are reported in MDD and with antidepressant use. The measure ignores amplitude scale and reference gain, so it should carry over to the external set, and it adds only 38 features.

I'm adding the two Hjorth parameters, mobility and complexity, for each channel and condition. They are computed on the 1–45 Hz signal, using the same filtering already done for the Higuchi fractal dimension. Mobility is the RMS frequency of the signal and complexity measures how far its waveform departs from a pure sine. Both are summaries of the whole spectrum and waveform. MDD studies report them as discriminative, and the model's fixed bands, alpha frequency and 1/f slope don't capture them directly. Both ignore amplitude scale, so they should carry over to the external amplifier. This adds only 76 features, a small step like the complexity and alpha-frequency features that were kept.

I'm adding per-channel weighted phase-lag index (wPLI) node strength for theta, alpha and beta in each condition: each channel's mean wPLI to every other channel. The covariance features are dominated by zero-lag coupling, which volume conduction and the reference inflate. wPLI keeps only consistent non-zero-lag phase coupling, which the model cannot currently see. Altered theta and alpha phase coupling is reported in MDD, and wPLI is largely insensitive to amplitude and reference, so it should carry over to the external amplifier. Summarising each channel as node strength adds only 114 features.

Hegerl's vigilance-regulation model links MDD to unusually stable, "hyperstable" EEG vigilance. That shows up as unusually low moment-to-moment fluctuation of alpha and theta, which all the current time-averaged features miss. So I'm adding one new family: for each channel and condition, the robust spread (IQR) of log relative theta and alpha power across 2 s epochs. Because it uses relative power, it ignores amplitude scale and gain, which should help on the external amplifier, and it adds only 76 features.

I'm adding one new feature family: the detrended fluctuation analysis (DFA) exponent of the theta and alpha amplitude envelopes, for each channel and condition. Linkenkaer-Hansen et al. (2005) reported that long-range temporal correlations in theta oscillations break down in MDD. That is a scale-free temporal-dynamics marker, which the time-averaged features and the IQR fluctuation features kept in round 13 can't capture. It ignores amplitude scale, and the window range is fixed in seconds, so it should carry over to the external amplifier. It adds 76 features.

I'm adding EEG microstate dynamics, a feature family the model has not used yet. The recordings are band-passed to 2–20 Hz and re-referenced to the common average, using that reference only for the microstate features. Four polarity-invariant template maps are fitted with modified k-means on GFP-peak (global field power) topographies pooled across all subjects, without labels. These templates are ordered against fixed A/B/C/D prototype maps built from the channel coordinates, so the class order stays consistent when the model is applied to new data. I then backfit the maps to each recording and compute, per class and condition, coverage, mean duration, occurrence rate and GEV (global explained variance), plus the probabilities of transitions between classes. MDD is reported to change microstate temporal dynamics, for example class D duration and coverage and the A↔D and C↔D transitions. These are sub-second whole-brain state switches, which the model's time-averaged spectral, connectivity and LRTC features do not capture. All of them ignore amplitude scale, and this adds 56 features.

I'm adding orthogonalized amplitude-envelope correlation (Hipp et al. 2012) for theta, alpha and beta, summarized as each channel's mean coupling to all other channels, per condition. Power-envelope coupling is a separate channel of communication from the phase coupling (wPLI) and zero-lag covariance the model already uses. Orthogonalizing removes zero-lag leakage from volume conduction and the reference, so it should carry over to the external clinic; the features ignore amplitude scale and add only 114 values.
